rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle signals amazement: if God's religion came through His messengers, where did this new religion come from?
rows.anchor: so from where has this new religion arrived?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question suggests the alleged associates fabricated a new religion without God's authorization.
rows.anchor: Do they have some associates who have fabricated a religion for them which was not permitted by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has no associates; the supposed partners and their religion are only a baseless notion.
rows.anchor: If they have some associates, then God has no associates.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi links the wording about the deferred decision to his discussion of the same expression in 42:14.
rows.anchor: is already mentioned in verse 14 above.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning means the wrongdoers would have been destroyed immediately if God had not fixed a time to decide their fate.
rows.anchor: had not the Almighty fixed a time to decide their fate, they would have been destroyed right away in this very world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their respite should prompt gratitude rather than arrogance; if they fail to use it, painful punishment awaits.
rows.anchor: the respite they have been given should not induce them to arrogance; in fact, they should show gratitude to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wrongdoers are idolaters who abandoned God's religion for polytheism and thereby wronged themselves.
rows.anchor: refers to the idolaters who had left the religion of God and had invented the new religion of polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters feel secure about the Hereafter because they assume their alleged deities will help them.
rows.anchor: today these idolaters have no fear of the Hereafter on the basis of their alleged deities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Hereafter, no one will intercede or help them, and each person will face the consequences of his deeds.
rows.anchor: there is no one to intercede or help them; every person will face his deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of the consequences will then be useless; punishment is unavoidable and their schemes cannot save them.
rows.anchor: people will fear the consequences of these deeds but this fear at that time will be of no avail

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who rely on faith and good deeds rather than deities will enter Paradise's orchards.
rows.anchor: lives having faith and doing good deeds instead of depending on their deities will find themselves in orchards of Paradise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise's believers will receive everything they desire from God.
rows.anchor: For them, from God will be everything which they want.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rawḍāt refers to the supplementary gardens and lawns within God's vast Paradise, provided for its inhabitants' enjoyment.
rows.anchor: refers to the supplementary orchards and lawns which will be found in the vast Paradise of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural wording reflects that Paradise contains multiple orchards and multiple gardens.
rows.anchor: Since there will be more than one orchard and more than one Paradise, both words in Arabic occur in the plural.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As the comparison with 42:20 shows, worldly people exaggerate present pleasures, while the true great blessing is God's gift on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: the real blessing which people should be after is the one which God will grant His servants on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The glad tidings of an eternal kingdom should move believers to strive for it and leave those enslaved to worldly pleasures alone.
rows.anchor: since the Almighty is giving the believers the glad tidings of an eternal kingdom, they should expend their effort to achieve it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads the exception as severed (munqaṭaʿ) and treats the following term as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: in my opinion is severed (munqaṭa‘) and the word Û is a verbal noun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's persistent call despite Quraysh hostility seeks no personal gain; he fulfills an obligation to bring his kin and people God's guidance and mercy first.
rows.anchor: fulfill the obligation which is imposed on him as a result of being part of a clan and tribe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets customarily begin preaching with their own tribes and nations, turning to others only after losing hope in them.
rows.anchor: the established practice of the prophets of God that they begin their preaching by first addressing the members

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was first directed to warn his near relatives, in keeping with the prophetic practice of addressing one's own kin first.
rows.anchor: It was a result of this practice that the Prophet (sws) was initially directed by the words:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet warned his Quraysh relatives, who led Arabia politically and religiously, about the Hereafter and persisted until their stubbornness exhausted hope.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) began his preaching mission by sounding a warning to them about the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only after Quraysh conspired to kill him did God direct the Prophet to migrate to Madīnah.
rows.anchor: they started to conspire to kill him, it is then when the Almighty directed him to migrate from them to Madīnah.

rows.speaker: Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī
rows.claim: Al-Farāhī reads the exception as a corrective clarification and, with 34:47, understands the Prophet's call about kinship and spending as serving the Quraysh's interests: wealth would pass from rich to poor, with no gain for him.
rows.anchor: Imām Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Farāhī views this verse differently. He is of the opinion that the exception is in the meaning of emendation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet barred himself and his relatives from benefiting from zakāh, removing any basis for suspicions about his motives.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) did not allow himself or his relatives to benefit from the zakāh money in any way

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi prefers his severed-exception reading but considers his mentor's emendation reading valid; the two are similar though not identical.
rows.anchor: Although I am convinced of my own interpretation, I do not regard my mentor’s interpretation to be incorrect.

rows.speaker: Generally, people
rows.claim: A common reading says the Prophet seeks kindness because of kinship; Islahi rejects it because asking for kind treatment would itself be a kind of reward.
rows.anchor: Generally, people have interpreted this verse to mean that the Prophet is stating

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All prophets denied seeking payment for preaching; none asked their people for kind treatment, since the preaching dispute allowed no compromise.
rows.anchor: No prophet has appealed to his respective nation to be dealt with kindly in return for his preaching

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh opposed the Prophet because of his call to monotheism and would have granted his wishes only if he abandoned it.
rows.anchor: The animosity of the Quraysh with the Prophet (sws) was because of his preaching

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet refused to stop preaching monotheism and told his opponents to do whatever they wished.
rows.anchor: openly told them that whatever they want to do they should carry on with it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He said he would not cease preaching even if given gold equal to Mount Uḥud.
rows.anchor: if he is given as much gold as the mountain of Uḥud, he will not desist from his preaching.

rows.speaker: Some misled sects
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the claim that the Prophet's requested reward was love for his relatives as contrary to the verse, other verses, and reason.
rows.anchor: Some misled sects have interpreted this verse to mean: “The only reward I ask you is to love my relatives.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Makkan setting makes that appeal implausible because most of the Prophet's relatives then sought his life.
rows.anchor: this verse belongs to the Makkan period when most of the Prophet’s near relatives were after his life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human piety benefits its doer, not God; God reinforces even small or large good deeds and rewards them with an eternal kingdom.
rows.anchor: whatever small or big good deed they do, God will increase and reinforce it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God forgives, values even the smallest good deed, nurtures it, and grants a great reward.
rows.anchor: He will not ignore the minutest of good deeds; in fact, He will increase it by nurturing and bestow it on His servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Quraysh accuse the Prophet of fabricating revelation to overawe people, the answer is that God gave him the Qur'an and could stop its flow whenever He willed.
rows.anchor: the Almighty Who has bestowed him with this fountain of graciousness, and whenever He wants He can stop its flow.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi supports this point by linking the passage to 17:86-87 in Sūrah Banī Isrā’īl.
